INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

Loops vs. Graphs, clearly explained!

loops are great, but they have a ceiling:

a loop makes one unit of work better. it cannot decide which units exist.

so you end up with a very good agent running the wrong three steps, in the wrong order, one at a time.

Graph engineering fixes this by moving the decision up a layer: what runs, what runs at the same time, and what never runs at all.

you need both. here's how it works:

a graph splits your system into two kinds of decision.

↳ inside a unit: the loop. produce, check, correct, repeat until green
↳ between units: the graph. split, fan out, merge, gate, send back

Prompts → Context → Harness → Loops → Graphs

you get parallel work, isolated contexts, and steps that stop running when nothing needs them.

the trick is being selective about what becomes a node.

only spend a model where judgment lives. merging, ranking, deduping and schema checks are edges, and edges are code. 

free, instant, and they cannot be argued out of a verdict. a graph where every edge is an agent pays rent on its own wiring.

one thing to know before you scale it.

a graph has two return paths, and almost everyone builds one.

↳ the correction edge is short. a gate rejects one unit back to the step that produced it, and it fixes the run you are in
↳ the learning edge is long. an accepted result goes back to the splitter as a constraint, and it fixes every run after

skip the second and you get a graph that is fast and never gets smarter. next week it starts from the same place with the same blind spots.

and a smaller one that eats whole nights: when a unit fails, return that unit, not the batch. 

send back four slices because one failed and you have just rewritten three correct ones. do it twice in a run and the run never converges.

You're in CRE.

You know you’re behind on AI.

But you don't know where to start.

This post is for you.

I've spent 200+ hours building CRE tools in Claude as a non-technical person. I use them every day on live deals.

Here's the Claude Starter Kit I wish I had on day 1:

Disclaimer: Claude will blow your mind, but will NOT solve your operational challenges on day 1.

Tinker, fail, have fun, learn the basics and go from there.

You know your business and will figure out where to focus, where to plug in to address your specific pain points.

But you can't get there if you don't start.

I promise the payoff will come. It has for me and just keeps compounding.

Here are five simple use cases, broken down by role, that show what Claude can do. I included pre-made prompts so you can start right away.

ACQUISITIONS

1) PDF => Excel

The simplest of all AI tricks, this is the one that got me hooked. Drop a PDF rent roll into Claude and see it turn it into Excel.

PROMPT: Turn this rent roll into one clean Excel      workbook. Include unit number, tenant name, unit type, square footage, current rent, market rent, move-in date, past-due balance, and a live upside column (market minus current). Add annual totals at the bottom and flag any tenant below 20% of market.

Next steps: This doesn’t just work for rent rolls of course. Drop in an OM and ask for the Pro Forma in excel, the lease abstract, whatever. This one you’ll find uses for right away.

2. Create neighborhood amenity maps for pitch decks

This was my first Skill, created out of pure annoyance that I couldn’t get Claude to easily recreate those POI maps it takes hours to create in Powerpoint.

But Claude is so good now, the Skill I built is already obsolete.

PROMPT: Create a branded amenity map for [property address]. Show transit stations, hotels, museums, major retailers, and restaurants within a 5-block radius. Show a maximum of five amenities for each category. Produce it as a standalone HTML file with a dark-mode sidebar and light-mode map tiles so I can open it in my browser and screenshot for a pitch deck.

(want my actual Skill that creates a more OM-ready version of the map? Shoot me a DM).

Next steps: These maps are amazing. Upload your Excel pipeline into Claude and ask for a dynamic map with key stats about each Pipeline property. You’ll be amazed at what comes up.

DUE DILIGENCE

3) Turn site visit voice notes into structured DD reports

Here’s another immediate winner. Ever leave a site walk, sit down at your desk, stare at half a page of scribbled notes and some janky iPhone photos and realize you lost 80% of what you just saw? No more.

Lots of ways to work this into your process, but here’s an easy one.

After the walk, go sit in your car and verbally brain dump everything you can remember into Claude. Just hit the voice record button and it will transcribe to text.

Next, copy the text into a new chat with the following prompt:

Organize this site visit transcript into a structured DD report. Categorize findings by roof, envelope, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, elevator, life safety, structural, and interior/common areas. For each category, summarize condition, flag urgency (immediate / Year 1 / defer), include estimated costs if discussed, and note where a vendor bid is still needed. List any categories not covered.

Distribute to your partners and they immediate know what you know.

Next steps: Record vendor feedback on site, drop third party reports into a running DD chat, there are dozens of ways to use Claude for DD but this simple brain dump exercise is the way to start.

4. Read any third-party report in plain English

Our latest SRA report was 67 pages. The PCA was 113. The ESA was 387.

Claude is good enough now to pick up the most important elements of these reports and call them out, summarize and explain in plan English. By all means double check the work, but this will save you a tremendous amount of time.

PROMPT: Summarize this report in plain English for an underwriting audience. What are the key findings, what would worry a lender, what capex should I add to my model, and what DD action items should go on my follow-up list? Flag anything that could move      pricing.

Next steps: Drop in any PDF, ask the same thing. Earnings reports and transcripts, SEC filings, OMs, market studies, etc.

Bonus Prompt for work order reports: Review this work order history and tell me what systemic issues the building has. Call out turnover patterns by unit, recurring maintenance categories, emergency response time red flags, and anything that points to deferred capex. Be underwriting-focused, not descriptive.

DATA/TREND ANALYSIS

5) Crunch any dataset

As a data hobbyist / nerd, this one also hooked me.

Claude runs code beneath what we all see, so as long as we ask the right questions, the math is (usually) right and Excel charts are a thing of the past.

Try this: Navigate to ApartmentList. com’s data page and download their nationwide rent estimates. Upload the CSV to Claude and ask the following:

Analyze rent trends for Austin, Houston, Dallas and San Antonio, normalizing data from 2020-2026, 2022-2026, 2024-2026 and for the past 12 months.

Pick any city you want, any time period. Immediate market insights.

I find these side by side city comparisons a super helpful way to see how certain factors (Covid, immigration, etc) impact cities differently. I can now choose any combo, for any time period with a simple text prompt.

Next steps: dump your expensive, janky CoStar data in and let Claude make sense of it.

--

If you got this far, you’re well on your way. Now, here are three tips for general Claude usage I figured out the hard way (ie trial and error).

1) Ask Claude to help

This is actually tips 1-100, it totally unlocked my Claude usage.

It turns out Claude is much better at using itself than you are, so ask it how. “I want you to help me underwrite deals without losing my personal touch, how can we work together?” “I need to collect rental comp data without breaking any laws – how can you help?”

Rather than trying to brute force Claude into following your low-brow human instructions, get Claude to write the prompts, write the instructions, create you a step-by-step guide.

Embrace the fact that this is, for our purposes, the smartest thing you’ll ever come in contact with – so use the hell out of it.

2) Use Projects for work you do more than once

A Project is a workspace where Claude can more easily do the same thing over and over again.

Projects accrue memory so it doesn't lose the script, and you can even have Claude write itself instructions to perform better and create (for example) due diligence reports in the same format every time.

I have projects for: Deal underwriting, rental comp      collection, portfolio analysis, due diligence and others.

For now, don’t worry too much about whether to use      Chat or CoWork – you’ll figure that out in time and you can move projects and chats back and forth between the two.

3) Promote good outputs back into your project knowledge

An early frustration of mine was that Claude’s output      was inconsistent. I’d ask for a DD report and the categories would be different every time, the graphs looked different, etc. This is an easy fix.

Grind through with Claude what you want the output to look like - remember you can relentless correct and improve and Claude  will just happily chug along like the good little sycophant it is and keep making the report better.

Once you have the format you like, save it and upload      it back into the project main page and ask Claude to add the report to its memory so whenever you ask for “DD report” you get the same thing.

There are more advanced and cleaner ways to do this      with Skills, etc but this is an easy start.

Here are my thoughts after looking at OMEGA60 by @Excellion 

JAN3 published OMEGA60 this month, a Bitcoin valuation model Samson Mow originally built in 2022 to price the future BTC holdings behind El Salvador's Bitcoin Bond against the fiat principal owed on it.

The headline is a 60% annual growth rate. I think that two other aspects deserve attention: the growth metric it runs on, and the fact that it deliberately stops projecting a dollar price at all.

MAGR (Median Annual Growth Rate)

Most models compound Bitcoin forward using CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) whereas, OMEGA60 uses MAGR, it's my first time learning about this metric.

CAGR is a geometric mean. Take the starting price, the ending price, and the number of years, and solve for the single constant rate that connects them:

CAGR = (End / Start)^(1/n) − 1
It uses exactly two data points. Everything that happened in between is invisible to it and as you can see only the endpoints matter.

MAGR is an order statistic. Compute each individual year's return, sort them, take the middle one. Every year contributes, but no single year can dominate, because rank is all that counts. A +1,300% year and a +95% year sit one slot apart in the ordering regardless of the gap between them.

Why that matters for Bitcoin

Bitcoin's annual returns from 2014 to 2022 were violent: −60.5%, +35.1%, +124.1%, +1,337.7%, −73.2%, +94.0%, +302.3%, +59.7%, −64.2%.

Sort them, take the middle: +59.7%. That is the entire derivation of the "60" in OMEGA60.

Now run the same window through CAGR. From the 2014 open to the 2022 close: 39.9%.

Then shorten the window to 2018–2022. The median is still 59.7% , the middle-ranked year doesn't move. Whereas the CAGR collapses to 3.6%.

JAN3's rolling five-year table makes the point harder. 2012–2016 gives a CAGR of 190% against a MAGR of 124%. Shift the window forward one year to 2013–2017 and the CAGR jumps to 300% while MAGR sits still at 124%. The CAGR moved 110 points because the window now ends on a cycle top. Nothing about Bitcoin's typical year changed.

That is endpoint sensitivity, and in a market with four-year boom-bust cycles it makes CAGR a measurement of when you started counting as much as of the asset.

CAGR's endpoint sensitivity is a bug for describing typical behaviour. It is not a bug for describing outcomes. CAGR is the only one of the two that reconstructs actual terminal wealth. If you compound 39.9% from Bitcoin's 2014 open for nine years, you land on the real 2022 close. If you compound the 59.7% median instead, you land around $55,000 — roughly 3.3x above where Bitcoin actually finished 2022.

The reason is mechanical. In log space, Bitcoin's crash years are more extreme than its median year is good. Three drawdowns of −60%, −64% and −73% impose a compounding penalty that a median simply discards, because the median only asks how many bad years there were, not how bad. Robustness to outliers is exactly what makes MAGR stable, and exactly what makes it structurally optimistic relative to realized returns.

The Terminus Zone

This is a very interesting and underrated concept, and I think it's getting less attention than the price target.

Every other long-horizon model (S2F, Power Law, Metcalfe, BITCOIN24) compounds a dollar price outward indefinitely and implicitly assumes Bitcoin and fiat coexist forever. If you push any of them far enough and they produce numbers that describe currency debasement rather than Bitcoin.

OMEGA60 draws a line and stops. The Terminus Line is defined as the price at which Bitcoin's market cap equals half of gold's. At roughly $31.5T for gold and ~20.07M coins outstanding, that's about $785,000 per bitcoin. OMEGA60's trajectory crosses it in August 2030.

Beyond that point, the model's claim is epistemic rather than numerical: the dollar stops being a reliable measuring stick for the thing being measured. The Weimar comparison in the piece is the right one. Gold didn't become harder money in 1923, the mark stopped functioning as a unit of account. A nominal price that goes vertical is telling you about the denominator.

Note also that the Terminus Line floats, and more than you'd think. It's pinned to gold's market cap, so it moves with both gold's price and the above-ground supply estimate  and that second input is soft. Published estimates of gold's total market cap currently run from roughly $32T to $34T, which shifts the Terminus Line from about $785K to somewhere north of $830K. Sources differ on above-ground tonnage by enough to move the number 20% on its own.

I think of this more of a feature, rather than a flaw: a relative monetary benchmark is more durable than a fiat target. But it means August 2030 is an estimate anchored to a moving reference.

Where it stands right now

Bitcoin is around $77K against an OMEGA60 value near $118K which is roughly 35% below trend.

That gap was 46% when JAN3 published on 17 August. A ~20% weekly rally has closed a quarter of it in six days, which is its own argument for treating this as a trajectory rather than a target. Worth remembering the model has never tracked cleanly: roughly 26% below at the end of 2016, 24% below in 2022, and 565% above in 2017, 240% above in 2020.

Deviation bands that wide are what I think are pretty good estimates of reading of a long-term trajectory model. They're also the reason it's hard to falsify on any timescale that matters to a trader. This is a framework for sizing sovereign exposure over a decade.

The convergence 

Four different models built on incompatible assumptions land in the same five-year window for $1M/BTC. S2F says May 2028. OMEGA60 says February 2031. BITCOIN24 says 2032. Power Law says June 2033.

Scarcity logic, median growth, tapering adoption curves, log-log regression, these four different theories of why, one narrow window for when. That convergence is either a real signal about the shape of monetization, or evidence that all four are quietly fitting the same historical curve.

I lean toward the former. But I'd hold that view loosely, and I'd read OMEGA60's 60% as a floor case.

Lagrange's trigonometric identities ✍️

This are one of those lovely mathematical discoveries which, on the surface, appears utterly complicated but in fact reveals a neat and elegant truth lying beneath all that seems messy and disorderly. In order to see what these identities are asserting, you first have to consider the unit circle, that is, a circle with a radius of exactly one unit placed at the centre of a flat coordinate plane. This circle is the setting in which the whole thing takes place and it is linked to trigonometry in a deep and beautiful manner. Any point located on the circumference of this circle can be fully described by an angle; if that angle is denoted by A, then the horizontal position of the point is given by the cosine of A and the vertical position by the sine of A. 

This means that cosine and sine are not merely abstract mathematical functions but actually represent the horizontal and vertical coordinates of points on the circle, which is the fundamental geometric basis of trigonometry. Now suppose that you place two points anywhere on the edge of this unit circle, one at angle A and the other at angle B, and then put to yourself two simple geometric questions. The first of these is: if you draw arrows from the centre of the circle to each of the two points and then add those arrows together by the usual rule of vector addition  that is, by joining the tail of one to the tip of the other to obtain a single resultant arrow what is the length of that resultant arrow? The second question is: if you draw a straight line from one point directly to the other across the circle, what is the length of that line, which mathematicians refer to as a chord? These two questions seem as though they should have complicated answers depending on all the particular details of where each point is situated on the circle, but the remarkable thing that Lagrange's identities show is that the answers depend on just one factor, namely the difference between the two angles, and are given by remarkably simple formulas involving trigonometric functions of half that angular difference. The first identity, known as the sum identity, answers the first question about the combined arrow and states that the square of the length of the resultant vector is equal to four times the square of the cosine of half the difference between the two angles. You can at once check that this works in the extreme cases. 

When both points are at the same place on the circle, so that the two angles are equal, the two arrows point in the same direction and add up perfectly to give a resultant of length two, so the square of the length should be four. Half the angular difference is zero, the cosine of zero is one, and four times one squared is four, which is exactly correct. When the two points are exactly opposite each other on the circle, so that the arrows point in precisely opposite directions, they completely cancel one another out and the resultant has zero length, so the square of the length should be zero. Half the angular difference is a quarter of a rotation, the cosine of a quarter rotation is zero, and four times zero squared is zero, which is also correct. For all the cases in between these two extremes, the formula gives the right answer precisely. The second identity, referred to as the difference identity, answers the second question about the chord and says that the square of the length of the chord joining the two points is equal to four times the square of the sine of half the angular difference. Once again you can easily verify the extreme cases. When the points coincide, the chord has zero length, half the angular difference is zero, the sine of zero is zero, and four times zero squared is zero, which is correct.

If Government Schools Need Secrecy, We Should Ask Why

A new order in Ayodhya bars outsiders—including YouTubers and people associated with social media—from entering government parishadiya schools or photographing/videographing inside them without prior permission. The education department says the restriction is intended to protect teaching, the dignity of teachers and the functioning of schools; it says authorised officials are already responsible for inspection and monitoring. 

But the timing deserves scrutiny.

The order comes amid a wider wave of student-led protests and public scrutiny of government schools, including complaints about drinking water, toilets, seating, food, teacher shortages and basic infrastructure. 

The accompanying video makes an important democratic point: if citizens are discovering deficiencies in public schools, the answer should be to fix the deficiencies—not make the deficiencies harder to see. 

There is, of course, a legitimate concern about outsiders disrupting classrooms or filming children and teachers without consent. That can—and should—be regulated.

But regulation must not become a shield against accountability.

These are government-funded schools.

They are not private estates.

They are sustained by taxpayers, and the children studying there are citizens whose right to decent education cannot depend upon whether outsiders are permitted to see the conditions in which they study.

If the government's inspection machinery is working perfectly, independent scrutiny should not be frightening.

In fact, it should be welcome.

A healthy system should be able to say:

“Come, inspect. Document the problem. Show us what we missed. We will fix it.”

The worrying alternative is:

“Don't enter. Don't record. Don't show.”

That does not automatically prove that something is being hidden. But it does create a transparency problem—particularly when the restriction follows growing public attention to deficiencies in government schools.

And this is bigger than Ayodhya.

When students themselves begin raising their voices about basic facilities, perhaps the question should not be:

“Who allowed them to speak?”

It should be:

“Why did they have to speak before the system listened?”

The state has the responsibility to provide functioning schools, adequate nutrition, safe drinking water, toilets, teachers and dignified learning environments.

Citizens should not have to become investigators to discover whether the state is doing its job.

And if independent scrutiny exposes a genuine problem, the appropriate response is not to silence the camera.

Fix what the camera found.

Because public education belongs to the public.

Transparency is not an attack on government.
Accountability is not anti-government.
And a citizen asking whether public money is producing a decent public service is not an outsider interfering in governance.

It is democracy doing its job.

Source/video: [Threads post](https://t.co/S3EQQKxpme)

Fact check: The Ayodhya order was issued on 19 August 2026 by the District Basic Education Officer and restricts unauthorised entry and photography/videography by outsiders, YouTubers and social-media personnel.

Gemini and Grok's view:
Optimistic asymmetric analysis (high-growth AI data engineering cash generator) and pessimistic asymmetric analysis (concentrated, high-multiple services business with dilution risk). Data drawn exclusively from Innodata’s Q2 2026 results (ended June 30, 2026; 8-K/press release August 6, 2026), Q1 10-Q, transcripts, and market data as of approximately August 20–21, 2026. No material new 8-K, Form 4, or warrant filings for INOD appeared in the last 24 hours (most recent major activity was the Q2 earnings release and related ATM equity program filing on/around August 6).

Core Facts Applied to the Three-Legged Stool (Both Analyses)
The Print: Q2 2026 revenue $92.1 million, +58% YoY (beats consensus). Q1 was $90.1 million, +54% YoY. This is accelerating sequential volume from AI data engineering programs. Full-year 2026 guidance reiterated at 40%+ revenue growth (with potential upside from unbooked large programs). Twelfth consecutive quarter of YoY growth.
The Backlog (Moat): Deferred revenue approximately $6.2 million as of June 30, 2026 (low absolute level; substantially all expected to convert within 12 months). No large multi-year remaining performance obligation quantified in filings. Growth is driven by expanding customer programs and volume rather than a large contractual backlog ratio. Customer prepayments boosted cash but create near-term delivery obligations. Ratio of deferred revenue to annualized revenue is low (<0.1x). This is closer to a list of active programs and hopes for conversion than fortress contracted cash.
The EBITDA Turn: Adjusted EBITDA positive and expanding for consecutive recent quarters (Q2 $25.4 million / 27.5% margin, +92% YoY; Q1 approximately $25 million / ~28%). Net income positive ($14.4 million in Q2). Operating cash flow strong in first half. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments $250.4 million (net ~$134 million after customer prepayments). Fully undrawn credit facility. Self-funding with substantial liquidity; no dilution required for survival (though an ATM equity program up to $300 million was filed).

Adjusted gross margin 49% (approaching software-like scalability). Current EV/Sales approximately 6.0x (EV ~$1.91 billion, TTM revenue ~$317 million); trailing P/E ~47–49x.

Architectural nuance (systems-level, not hardware): Innodata provides data engineering and AI systems services focused on high-quality training, post-training, evaluation, and deployment data for advanced AI models, including agentic reinforcement learning environments, benchmarks, and domain-specific datasets. The underlying architecture combines proprietary tooling, human-in-the-loop processes, and IP-owned off-the-shelf datasets that interact at a systems level with frontier model training pipelines (data quality, annotation consistency, evaluation harnesses). Not easily plug-and-played by generic BPO or crowd-sourced alternatives because of specialized quality controls, domain expertise, and multi-year process IP required by frontier labs. Primary source for certain high-complexity AI data workflows.

Capacity allocation & supply-chain chokepoints: IP is owned in proprietary platforms, datasets, and processes; physical capacity is primarily skilled workforce and tooling (scalable via hiring/offshore delivery centers). No fab/foundry dependency. Pricing power exists in specialized, high-value programs during demand spikes from AI labs.

Qualification cycles & forward modeling: Already in commercial volume ramp with frontier and Big Tech customers (multiple expanding programs). Current revenue is primarily production-scale AI data engineering rather than pure NRE; further agentic/RL and physical AI programs are in early commercial stages with 2026–2027 visibility.

Downstream M&A / TAM expansion: Services model expanding into higher-value research-driven products (benchmarks, RL environments, cybersecurity training suites) and platforms rather than remaining pure component/data supplier. Leadership transition (Rahul Singhal to CEO effective September 30, 2026) supports this.

No material oil exposure or energy moat. Activation lag for capacity is low-to-moderate (workforce scaling measured in months). Short interest approximately 14% of float—elevated and a potential squeeze candidate on continued beats.

Optimistic Analysis (Asymmetric Upside as AI Data Cash-Printing Utility)
Revenue is accelerating sharply (+58% in Q2) with operating leverage (Adj EBITDA +92%). Deferred revenue is modest but active programs and customer diversification (largest customer down to 37%, new Big Tech at 34%, plus frontier lab win) provide momentum. Multiple consecutive quarters of strong positive adjusted EBITDA and robust cash generation confirm self-funding utility status. Gross margins near 50% support scalability. Floor is cash generation and growth trajectory rather than pure hype. Bottleneck solved: high-friction need for high-quality, specialized training/evaluation data and agentic environments that generic providers cannot reliably deliver at frontier-lab standards. Low activation lag. Institutional solvency green light is firmly on. Passes all three legs. Binary verdict: BUY.

Pessimistic Analysis (Asymmetric Downside as Concentrated High-Multiple Services Risk)
Growth is real and accelerating but highly concentrated (two customers ~71% of Q2 revenue) and project/volume-driven rather than locked multi-year backlog (deferred revenue only ~$6 million; ratio low). Adjusted EBITDA is strongly positive, yet the ATM filing signals potential future dilution. Gross margins approach software levels but the model remains services-heavy with workforce scaling risks. Valuation EV/Sales ~6x and P/E ~48x represent a premium to many IT services peers; justified only if 40%+ growth sustains—otherwise a hype premium on AI narrative. Customer concentration creates single-point fragility; Tier-1 AI labs have alternative data providers. No regulatory inventory bottlenecks of note, but delivery obligations from prepayments exist. Short interest elevated adds volatility. The backlog leg is the weakest (order/program visibility rather than large contracted cash). Binary verdict if strict on fortress backlog: AVOID (or wait for clearer multi-customer backlog conversion and reduced concentration); the missing/weak leg is quantified long-duration contracted backlog.

Unified verdict under the framework: High-growth AI data engineering business that has achieved the print and EBITDA legs with strong self-funding cash flow, but the backlog leg is modest in contractual terms. Solvency test is clearly passed (large cash position, positive cash generation, undrawn facility). Binary institutional recommendation on solvency plus current evidence: BUY, with explicit note that the backlog is program-driven rather than multi-year RPO-style contracted cash. Simple PEG over a 2026–2028 window is elevated on trailing metrics but compresses meaningfully if 30–40%+ compounding materializes. Next catalysts include Q3 results and conversion of the large potential programs excluded from current guidance.

Innodata Inc. (NASDAQ: INOD) Analysis

SEC Filings & Capital Flow Trajectory (August 21, 2026)
Recent SEC filings, specifically the Form 8-K and Form 10-Q filed on August 6, 2026, confirm Q2 2026 revenue of $92.1 million alongside the initiation of a new equity distribution agreement (S-3 shelf registration) managed by Goldman Sachs and others. Capital flows demonstrate immense operating cash generation ($164.4 million in H1 2026), heavily driven by customer advances. Institutional capital momentum is surging, actively pivoting from legacy SaaS and BPO providers toward AI-infrastructure data components, which is reflected in the massive capital inflows and subsequent stock repricing following the Q2 earnings print.

Analysis 1: Deep-Tech & Asymmetric Investing Framework (Optimistic)

The Three-Legged Stool (Must-Pass Criteria)

The Print: Q2 2026 revenue achieved $92.1 million, accelerating to a 58% YoY growth rate. This marks the 12th consecutive quarter of YoY growth, firmly establishing a rapid, structural revenue ramp.

The Backlog (The Moat): While traditional "backlog" metrics vary in services, INOD's contracted cash moat is validated by the $164.4 million in H1 2026 operating cash flow, bolstered by substantial customer prepayments for AI data services. This signifies "contracted cash" funded directly by frontier labs rather than a "list of hopes."
The EBITDA Turn: The company recorded $25.4 million in Adjusted EBITDA in Q2 (representing 27.5% of revenue), an increase of 92% YoY. They are entirely self-funding operations, holding $250.4 million in cash and short-term investments with zero outstanding debt.
Margin & Valuation (The Floor)

EV/Sales & P/E Multiples: INOD currently trades at a P/E of ~46.7x. Compared to legacy data/BPO peers like TaskUs (TASK) or Telus International (TIXT), which trade at 10x–15x multiples, INOD carries a structural tech premium. Relative to high-growth AI-infrastructure peers, the valuation is mathematically supported by the 92% YoY EBITDA growth.

Floor: The floor is rigidly supported by $134 million in net cash (excluding customer prepayments) and rapidly expanding profitability.
Gross Margins: Q2 Adjusted Gross Margin expanded to 49% (surpassing the 40% long-term target), indicating a successful transition from low-margin manual annotation to software-like scalability through reusable, proprietary datasets.
The Bottleneck & Catalyst

High-Friction Problem: Frontier AI labs face a critical bottleneck: the exhaustion of high-quality, human-validated training data (RLHF) required to prevent model collapse. INOD explicitly solves this data scarcity chokepoint.

Swing/Stranded Asset: It operates as a swing asset, remaining entirely independent of energy market shocks or physical supply chain disruptions.
Activation Lag: Near-zero. The company is actively scaling capacity; its primary "Big Tech" client grew from 17% of revenue in Q1 to 34% in Q2, demonstrating rapid capacity deployment and absorption.
The Ape-In Test

Solvency: An institutional "green light" is definitively on, driven by flawless solvency metrics (zero debt, massive cash generation).

Regulatory Bottlenecks: Negligible inventory turnover risks exist, as the "inventory" consists of digital data and human capital.
Verdict: BUY. The company successfully clears the print, backlog, and EBITDA turn requirements with expanding operating margins.
Deep-Tech Nuance Avoidance Criteria

Architectural Nuance vs. Spec Sheets: INOD does not sell hardware specs; it provides the structural data architecture for Large Language Models (LLMs). Its systems-level integration involves embedding proprietary human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflows directly into the pre-training and alignment phases of frontier models. Competitors cannot easily "plug-and-play" because INOD's domain-specific datasets (medical, legal, technical) require verified expert credentials that take years to aggregate and validate.

Capacity Allocation & Supply Chain Chokepoints: INOD owns the intellectual property of its off-the-shelf datasets, which can be licensed multiple times across different customers. The true "fab capacity" here is access to highly skilled subject-matter experts. INOD holds the pricing power as AI labs bid aggressively for exclusive access to premium, non-synthetic data pipelines.
Qualification Cycles & Forward Modeling: INOD has passed the NRE/development phase and is currently executing a commercial volume ramp. Big Tech adoption is confirmed in the Q2 2026 data. Valuation must forward-model the reuse of its proprietary datasets, avoiding backward-looking BPO metrics.
Downstream M&A and TAM Expansion: The company is actively expanding down the stack by shifting from a purely outsourced labor model to an IP-ownership model (proprietary data licensing), vastly expanding its TAM and transitioning from a component supplier to a subsystem ecosystem.
Analysis 2: Asymmetric Framework - Devil's Advocate (Pessimistic)

1. Market Health Review: The broader indexes remain above the 8 and 21 EMAs, flagging a healthy systemic macro environment, though AI-infrastructure equities are facing increased scrutiny regarding CapEx returns.

2. The Three-Legged Stool (Screener):

Undervalued: Fails. With a P/E of 46.7x, it is not undervalued relative to its historical peer group. The valuation floor is dictated entirely by the continuation of AI CapEx spending by a concentrated group of buyers.

Rapid Revenue Ramp: Passes. Q2 YoY growth of 58% confirms the machine is working.

Hot Sector: Passes. The sector possesses extreme institutional momentum.
Strategic Pivot: The latest earnings transcript reveals a massive CapEx and operational pivot from legacy document processing to AI infrastructure design wins. Management emphasizes "pre-training programs" and "off-the-shelf datasets," actively distancing the firm from legacy unit metrics.
3. Devil's Advocate & The Ape-In Test:
Reviewing the 10-Q data reveals a critical fragility: extreme customer concentration. In Q2 2026, two customers accounted for 71% of total revenue (37% and 34%) and 66% of accounts receivable. Furthermore, the August 6, 2026 Form 8-K filing of an equity distribution agreement signals management's readiness to dilute shareholders to raise capital at these elevated levels, contradicting the narrative of self-sustaining cash flow. Comparing the 46.7x P/E against peers trading closer to 15x identifies this as a "hype premium."

The Ape-In Test: Assessing strictly on solvency, it passes. Assessing on risk-adjusted client concentration, it fails.
4. The Bottleneck & Catalyst:

Bottleneck: Solves the human-validated data bottleneck for LLMs.

EBITDA Turn: Achieved ($25.4 million in Q2).

Geopolitical Fragility: A significant portion of INOD's annotation workforce operates offshore (e.g., Philippines, India). Should global regulatory hurdles regarding AI data sovereignty or cross-border data flows emerge, this structural labor arbitrage transforms into a regulatory bottleneck.
Plan B: Tier 1 customers possess a clear 'Plan B' (utilizing Scale AI, Snorkel, or bringing data generation strictly in-house via synthetic data). If synthetic data generation eclipses human-in-the-loop workflows, INOD's pricing power drops to zero.
5. The Forward Looking Pivot:
The company proves product-market fit, but the risk remains that the current quarter's cash flow is artificially inflated by customer prepayments that will amortize, leaving a fundamental gap if Big Tech halts model training runs.

6. Execution & Risk:
Dilution Check: Cash runway is safe, but the newly filed S-3 shelf registration poses an immediate dilution overhang.

Negative Asymmetry: The stock is "priced for perfection." Any loss of either of the two major clients would instantly compress the multiple by 50% or more.

7. Technical Confluence:
The chart displays violent post-earnings expansion with massive volume spikes following the Q2 print. The asset is currently extended far above structural support levels. Consequently, determine this is not a 75% 'Ape In' entry point; a reversal signal or consolidation base is strictly required.

8. Stranded Asset vs. Swing Asset:
It operates as a swing asset in the digital realm, isolated from $100/barrel oil dynamics, focusing purely on compute and data ecosystems.

9. Energy Moat:
No physical energy moat exists. Its proprietary infrastructure relies on human capital and digital data rights.

10. Activation Lag:
Activation lag is low for software deployment, but scaling human experts for complex legal or medical data annotation takes multiple quarters, presenting a friction point for rapid capacity expansion.

11. Short Squeeze Candidate:
Given historical volatility and skepticism around legacy BPOs pivoting to AI tech valuations, it remains a battleground stock. Any slight miss on forward guidance will attract aggressive short-selling, though current momentum has forced recent covering.

12. Output:
AVOID. The "Backlog/Moat" leg of the stool is highly fragile. While the utility is currently generating cash, the extreme concentration of 71% of revenue tied to just two clients, combined with the existential threat of synthetic data replacing human annotators, presents asymmetric downside risk at a 46x multiple.

13. PEG Ratio:
Assuming EPS compounding stabilizes at ~25% annually after the initial AI hyper-growth phase, the forward PEG ratio (2026-2028) sits at approximately 1.8x, suggesting the valuation is slightly overextended relative to realistic, multi-year compounding rates.

Free speech spine intact: Art.19(1)(a); limits only under Art.19(2)—sovereignty, integrity (via 16th Amend., 1963), public order, decency, contempt, defamation, incitement.

Shreya Singhal (2015): struck 66A IT Act; mandated narrow tests (“incitement”, “tendency to create”). Sincerity space preserved.

Right to know fuels deliberation: PUCL v. Union (2003) & ADR (2002)—candidate disclosures as Art.19(1)(a); RTI Act 2005 operationalises truth access, not performance.

State coercion checked: Anuradha Bhasin (2020)—internet restrictions must be proportional, reasoned, reviewable. Kaushal Kishor (2023)—remedies exist for ministerial speech harm; no blanket gag on political speech.

Harmful speech contained, not chilled: Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation to protect Art.21 reputation; Amish Devgan (2020) clarified hate-speech thresholds—ethics by law, not by vibe.

Platform due-diligence (not censorship): IT (Intermediary Guidelines & Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021—grievance officers, 36-hr takedown on court/LEA orders, traceability for heinous crimes; 69A IT Act blocking only via speaking orders + review (per Shreya Singhal).

Election truth-checks: Model Code of Conduct, cVIGIL, paid-news rules; ECI + SVEEP strengthen voter information.

Civic transparency expanding: Open Government Data, Proactive RTI (s.4), Social Audit (MNREGA/SSA rules)—institutionalise fact visibility.

Bottom line: The architecture prizes sincerity by rights (19(1)(a)), guardrails (19(2)), remedies (courts/RTI/ECI). The market is noisy; the constitution makes it corrigible.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

Elon Musk (@elonmusk) is making a renewed push for Starlink in India, arguing that the satellite internet service could help connect people in rural areas that remain underserved by traditional broadband networks.

Musk said Starlink could benefit the “least served” parts of India, particularly rural communities. Government data shows a significant connectivity gap between urban and rural areas despite more than 1 billion internet subscriptions nationwide.

India had about 440.9 million rural internet subscriptions as of March, compared with roughly 651.9 million in urban areas. Rural internet subscription density stood at 48.31 per 100 people versus 126.80 in cities.

The comments come as SpaceX ($SPCX) reportedly reapplied for Indian regulatory approval to deploy its second-generation Starlink constellation. The proposed network could include nearly 30,000 satellites and direct-to-device capabilities.

Starlink already received an Indian telecom license in 2025 and approval for its first-generation constellation. SpaceX has also reached distribution agreements with major telecom providers Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio.

India has invested heavily in rural connectivity through BharatNet, laying more than 850,000 route-kilometers of fiber and making roughly 221,000 local government areas service-ready. However, last-mile connectivity remains incomplete in many locations.

Musk sees low-Earth-orbit satellites as a way to reach regions where deploying towers or fiber is too expensive or difficult. Direct-to-device technology could eventually extend connectivity directly to compatible smartphones.

Starlink still faces regulatory, security and infrastructure requirements before commercial service can fully launch, but India represents one of the company’s largest potential growth markets.

Starlink is no longer just expanding It is steadily surrounding India. 🇮🇳

It is already operational in Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, while Nepal is also moving towards adoption. Every neighbour India has except China is either on Starlink or getting there.

Now connect the dots.

Over the past few years governments changed in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

Each time, Starlink was not just embedded but actively used to keep protest movements connected when those governments tried to shut the internet down.

We have seen in Iran exactly how US-controlled satellite internet becomes an operational tool the moment a government tries to cut its own network.

Starlink bypasses ground infrastructure entirely, No government can filter, monitor or cut it through conventional means once it is being used.

China looked at this exact scenario and banned Starlink entirely and It built its own satellite internet through the Thousand Sails constellation instead. 

India currently holds Starlink at the licensing stage and has not yet allowed full commercial rollout.

Pausing is the right instinct but it is not a permanent answer. India needs to decide now, before the rollout begins, whether it wants a US-controlled satellite network operating on its soil or whether it takes China's approach and shuts the door completely.

SOUTH KOREA BANS POLYMARKET

South Korea's media regulator has voted to permanently block access to Polymarket, the blockchain-based prediction market platform, deeming it an illegal gambling service. The Korea Communications Standards Commission (KCSC) ruled on August 18 that the platform's winner-take-all profit structure—where users bet on political, economic, sports and weather outcomes—fosters a "speculative mindset". Polymarket argued it had removed Korean-language services and Korean won payments, and that its peer-to-peer, non-custodial structure means it has "no central operator". The KCSC rejected this, stating that "application of domestic laws cannot be evaded based on technical characteristics".

THE WINNER-TAKE-ALL PROBLEM

The KCSC found that Polymarket's model constitutes information that "abets gambling" under the Criminal Act and "similar acts" under the National Sports Promotion Act. The commission consulted the National Police Agency, the National Gambling Control Commission and the Korea Sports Promotion Foundation—all of which agreed the platform's operations could constitute the crime of gambling. A key factor: Polymarket had even hosted markets on "Seoul precipitation levels in August"—events entirely beyond users' control. The platform's operators manage markets, set trading rules and collect transaction fees through cryptocurrency deposit and settlement systems, creating a "practical illegal gambling environment for domestic users".

JOINING THE GLOBAL CRACKDOWN

South Korea now joins more than 30 jurisdictions that have restricted Polymarket. France blocked access in July 2026, citing risks of "massive losses" and "betting manipulation". Australia and Germany imposed blocks in August and September 2025. Spain, Indonesia, Argentina, Brazil and India have all taken action this year. The platform currently lists 39 countries with fully restricted access. Polymarket's defense—that its decentralized, non-custodial structure exempts it from domestic law—has failed. Regulators are sending a clear message: decentralized does not mean unregulatable. The global crackdown on prediction markets is accelerating.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

FREE SPEECH IS NOT DEAD — RESISTANCE IS STILL ALIVE

Former The Hindu Editor-in-Chief N. Ram makes an important distinction: India today is not living through the kind of total censorship that existed during the Emergency. The danger is real, but so is the space for resistance.

His argument is powerful because India’s strength lies in its enormous diversity and pluralism. A country this vast cannot easily be silenced when an independent press, citizens and social-media platforms continue to create spaces for dissent.

The recent Cockroach Janata Party protest movement illustrates that point. Whatever one thinks of the language, excesses or political direction of such movements, the very ability of citizens to organise, speak, protest and challenge authority demonstrates that the state has not succeeded in controlling the entire public sphere.

But N. Ram also raises the harder question: How long can spontaneous resistance survive without organisation, persistence and democratic purpose?

That is where the responsibility of citizens begins.

Free speech is not merely the freedom to speak when the government permits it. It is the freedom to question power, ridicule authority, expose wrongdoing and disagree without fear.

Democracy does not die only when censorship becomes absolute. It also weakens when citizens voluntarily surrender their courage, when the press abandons independence, and when dissent becomes socially or politically inconvenient.

The lesson is therefore simple:

Protect the space for dissent before someone closes it. Defend free speech even when the speech is uncomfortable. And never confuse the absence of total censorship with the presence of a healthy democracy.

The real test of freedom is not whether the powerful can speak freely, but whether the powerless can still speak truth to power.

Nine years ago, the Supreme Court affirmed that privacy is a fundamental right for every Indian. This August, we're marking that milestone, along with the sixth edition of Privacy Supreme, IFF's annual flagship convening.

This year, in collaboration with @thewire_in, we're trading panels and podiums for real conversations. Journalists, researchers, and young advocates come together to unpack what privacy actually looks like in our everyday digital lives.

text:
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has proposed making Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication systems mandatory for specified vehicles. V2V can improve road safety by allowing vehicles to exchange information such as speed, position and direction to prevent collisions. But an always-on system can also create a new infrastructure for tracking and surveillance. (1/5)
Read More: https://t.co/YckNaxIuq6

We have also raised concerns about centralised authentication systems. If a central authority can link a pseudonymous vehicle identifier back to a real vehicle, it could potentially reconstruct who is travelling where and when. Privacy should therefore be built into the technical architecture through decentralised systems, including technologies such as zero-knowledge credentials and secure hardware. (4/5)

IFF has urged MoRTH to ensure that V2V data cannot be centrally logged, intercepted, retained or repurposed for tracking, surveillance or law enforcement without specific legal authorisation and judicial oversight. Independent security and privacy audits should happen before mandatory deployment, followed by periodic reviews of whether the mandate remains necessary and proportionate. Safer roads should not mean building a new surveillance infrastructure. (5/5)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

text: There is also a serious question about the databases being used. Delhi Police previously said facial recognition databases were maintained under a statute that Parliament has since repealed. Meanwhile, CP PLUS has publicly stated that it developed the Ikshana vehicle with Delhi Police. The legal basis for these databases, and what access private vendors have to facial data, remains unclear. (4/5)

Peaceful assembly is a constitutional right. Surveillance that identifies and profiles protesters can create a chilling effect on that right, especially when there are no clear rules, retention limits, privacy assessments or disclosed safeguards. The protest may have ended, but the question remains: where are the faces collected at Jantar Mantar now, who can access them, and under what law? (5/5)

The @ttindia edit is correct in its warning. Nowhere else in the world does census include this. @internetfreedom has already raised this issue, explaining in detail what the problem is. https://t.co/l9lBObPozN

NIXI has now given a third explanation for suspending https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP. First it was “Invalid WHOIS”. Then a “critical keyword”. Now, three weeks into the suspension, it says “Sansad” is a reserved term for Constitutional Authorities. But NIXI’s own reserved names list does not reserve “sansad” as a term, and https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP is not on it. (1/8)
Read More: https://t.co/BSrSHIC1hf

The purpose of reserved names is to prevent impersonation of public institutions. “Sansad” is also an ordinary Hindi word, and “Chalo Sansad” was the reported name of a public protest. The website expressly disclaimed any affiliation with Parliament or the Government. Reserving https://t.co/vWkHekQQYB for the official Digital Sansad website does not mean citizens cannot lawfully refer to Parliament in a domain name. (7/8)

Today, acting on the registrant’s instructions, IFF through Apar Gupta, Advocate sent a rejoinder to NIXI. We have placed the inconsistencies, the 2004 policy, NIXI’s own reserved-name lists, the RDAP comparison and the Aadhaar concerns on record. We have again demanded restoration, disclosure of the legal basis and any underlying orders, accountability for the Aadhaar collected, and functional grievance channels. As of 17 August, https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP remains suspended. We will publish any further response. (8/8)
Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

But Clause 3.4.6 does not say that a registered domain can be suspended. It says certain names will be reserved “prior to the opening of registration”. The suspension provision in the 2004 Framework is elsewhere, and NIXI does not invoke it. A power to reserve a name before registration is not automatically a power to suspend a live domain years later. (3/8)

More importantly, NIXI’s own published ASCII Reserved Names list reserves four exact “sansad” domains: https://t.co/vWkHekQQYB, https://t.co/sffuML4CXk, https://t.co/2rEVGLFZf9 and https://t.co/aSsed0ZeGh. https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP is not one of them. There is also no published rule saying that every domain which merely incorporates a reserved word becomes prohibited. (4/8)
The government has all data on Aadhaar, Voter IDs, Passport so why is this information relevant for a census?

quotedTweet.text:
IFF has written to the Union Home Secretary and the Census Commissioner over the household survey notified four days ago. Serial numbers 36 to 40 ask for mobile, Aadhaar, voter ID and passport numbers, not whether you have them, unlike serial number 40, which only asks about availability of a driving license.

IFF supports enumerating caste for substantive equality. But pairing Aadhaar numbers with religion and caste sits against the Aadhaar Act's bar on profiling, and the questionnaire itself remains unpublished.
We are not opposed to the census. We want it conducted in a way that earns public trust.
